title: Agoda Replaces 72-Shard SQL Server Price Cache with DragonflyDB
gist: Agoda migrated its 1.5TB, 300K-reads/1.5M-writes-per-second hotel price cache from a 72-shard SQL Server deployment to DragonflyDB, cutting P99 read latency roughly eightfold and replacing manual shard management with cluster-based scaling and decentralized failover.

themes.theme: Why SQL Server sharding broke down

insights.claim: Agoda's price cache previously ran on 72 manually sharded Microsoft SQL Server instances requiring application-level shard routing, and after doubling hardware capacity in early 2024 the team was again approaching capacity limits within a year.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Shows the operational ceiling of manually sharded relational databases under fast-growing write-heavy workloads — a recurring cost driver for any e-commerce/travel platform scaling pricing or inventory caches.
insights.quote: It became clear that continuing to add resources to SQL Server was not a viable or cost-effective long-term strategy.
insights.locator: Agoda's previous architecture required application-level shard routing

insights.claim: The SQL Server-based cache required a separate cleanup process just to remove expired supplier pricing data, adding operational overhead beyond the core scaling problem.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Highlights a hidden cost of general-purpose relational stores for volatile/expiring data — built-in TTL/key-expiration in newer in-memory stores directly eliminates this class of maintenance work.
insights.locator: The growing workload also required a separate cleanup process

insights.claim: Agoda selected DragonflyDB over SQL Server because its shared-nothing, multithreaded architecture, Redis compatibility, cluster-based scaling, and built-in key expiration matched the price cache's MGET/SET-heavy workload, and the team validated this against workload-specific benchmarks (memtier_benchmark with a 1:6 read-to-write ratio and 10-key average MGET) rather than relying on published vendor benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A reusable evaluation pattern for infra teams: reproduce production access patterns with tools like memtier_benchmark rather than trusting generic vendor benchmarks before a migration decision.
insights.locator: The team evaluated DragonflyDB against the workload

insights.claim: After migration, DragonflyDB served roughly 300,000 read requests per second at about 8 milliseconds P99 latency, an approximately eightfold improvement in P99 read latency versus the prior SQL Server architecture.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Concrete before/after latency benchmark (8x P99 improvement) investors can use to gauge DragonflyDB's competitive edge over legacy relational caches in real production traffic, not synthetic tests.
insights.locator: Following the migration, Agoda reported an approximately eightfold improvement

insights.claim: The full DragonflyDB cluster, expanded to a three-shard-per-cluster design holding the complete 1.5TB dataset, processed approximately 1.6 million writes per second at around 10 milliseconds P99 latency.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Demonstrates DragonflyDB's throughput ceiling in a real high-write travel-pricing workload (1.6M writes/sec), a useful benchmark reference for competitors like Redis Enterprise or Valkey evaluating similar migrations.
insights.locator: The team subsequently moved to a three-shard-per-cluster design

insights.claim: Agoda's initial single 1TB DragonflyDB deployment pushed toward the 90% memory-safety threshold as data grew organically, forcing a redesign to a three-shard cluster before full migration could proceed — showing even incremental in-memory migrations need headroom planning.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A cautionary data point for capacity planning: initial in-memory cache sizing based on current data volume can be outgrown quickly, requiring re-architecture mid-migration.
insights.locator: Agoda initially deployed a 1 TB DragonflyDB instance

insights.claim: Before cutting over traffic, Agoda ran dual reads comparing SQL Server and DragonflyDB by checking supplier counts and price-data lengths (not full payloads) as Prometheus metrics, achieving over 99.9% parity on both dimensions before proceeding.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A practical, lower-cost parity-validation pattern (checking structural proxies instead of full payload diffs) that other teams can reuse for large-scale datastore migrations to reduce risk without high compute overhead.
insights.locator: Before shifting customer traffic, Agoda introduced dual reads

insights.claim: Agoda used an A/B experiment to gradually shift customer traffic to DragonflyDB, reaching 100% migration after several weeks before retiring the SQL Server read and write paths entirely.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Confirms a gradual A/B traffic-shift methodology as the de-risking standard for critical-path datastore swaps at scale.
insights.locator: Agoda then used an A/B experiment

insights.claim: Instead of a central coordinator, Agoda's two-cluster (A/B) high-availability design has each application pod independently compare cache-hit ratios across clusters using five minutes of local observations; a statistically significant 10-percentage-point divergence marks a cluster unreadable, while recovery requires the gap to shrink to within three percentage points.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A concrete decentralized-consensus pattern (asymmetric failover/recovery thresholds, no central coordinator) that reduces single-point-of-failure risk — a reusable architecture reference for other high-availability cache designs.
insights.locator: Instead of relying on a central coordinator

insights.claim: In an outage simulation, roughly 40 application pods independently detected the failure and completed failover within approximately two minutes without manual intervention.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Quantifies the operational payoff of decentralized failover: sub-2-minute automated recovery across dozens of pods, a benchmark for evaluating similar HA designs elsewhere.
